prompt: Jahn–Teller distortions arise from unequally occupied degenerate orbitals. For a pair of degenerate orbitals, which electron counts leave them unequally occupied?

choices.text: One or three electrons
Two or four electrons
choices.why: Even numbers divide evenly between two orbitals, so two or four electrons give equal occupancy.

choices.text: Only zero electrons
choices.why: Empty orbitals are equally occupied. Unequal occupancy needs an electron count that can't be split evenly: one or three.

choices.text: Any number of electrons, since degenerate orbitals are always unequally filled
choices.why: Two or four electrons can be shared evenly between two orbitals; only one or three cannot.

explanation: With two degenerate orbitals, two or four electrons can be divided evenly, giving equal occupancy. One or three electrons cannot, so the orbitals are unequally occupied. Lowering the symmetry splits the pair; with three electrons, two can then sit lower and one higher, for a net drop in energy.

prompt: Which octahedral d-electron configuration is expected to show a strong Jahn–Teller distortion?

choices.text: Low-spin d7
Low-spin d6
choices.why: Low-spin d6 is t2g6 eg0: both sets are equally occupied, so there is no driving force for distortion.

choices.text: High-spin d5
choices.why: High-spin d5 is t2g3 eg2, one electron in each orbital, so every degenerate set is equally occupied.

choices.text: d8
choices.why: d8 is t2g6 eg2, which fills the eg pair evenly with one electron each.

explanation: Strong Jahn–Teller distortions are seen for high-spin d4, low-spin d7 and d9. Low-spin d7 is t2g6 eg1: the single eg electron leaves the two degenerate eg orbitals unequally occupied.

prompt: High-spin d6 (t2g4 eg2) has unequally occupied t2g orbitals, yet it is not one of the configurations that show strong Jahn–Teller distortions. Why are strong effects associated with unequal occupancy of eg instead?

choices.text: The eg orbitals are the ones involved in σ bonding, so their energies respond strongly to bond lengths
The t2g orbitals are higher in energy than the eg orbitals
choices.why: In octahedral geometry the eg set lies above t2g. The distinction is about σ bonding, not which set is higher.

choices.text: The eg set holds more electrons than the t2g set
choices.why: The eg set has two orbitals and t2g has three. What matters is that eg is linked to σ bonding and hence bond length.

choices.text: Unequal occupancy of t2g orbitals is impossible
choices.why: It happens, as in high-spin d6. It just doesn't produce strong distortions, because t2g isn't tied to σ bonding.

explanation: In octahedral geometry, strong Jahn–Teller effects appear when the unequally occupied orbitals are in the eg set rather than the t2g set. The eg set is linked to σ bonding, so its orbitals are strongly influenced by the strength of that bonding interaction, and hence by the bond length.

prompt: An octahedral d9 complex distorts by lengthening its two axial (z-axis) bonds. Which d orbitals drop slightly in energy?

choices.text: dz2, dxz and dyz, the orbitals that interact with ligands along the z axis
dx2−y2 and dxy, which lie in the xy plane
choices.why: These orbitals rise slightly, keeping the average orbital energy at the barycenter.

choices.text: Only dx2−y2
choices.why: dx2−y2 points at the equatorial ligands, which have not moved away; it rises slightly.

choices.text: All five d orbitals drop by the same amount
choices.why: The average orbital energy is preserved at the barycenter, so some orbitals rise when others fall.

explanation: Elongating the axial bonds weakens interactions along z, slightly lowering dz2, dxz and dyz. The other orbitals, dx2−y2 and dxy, rise slightly because the average energy of the orbitals is preserved at the barycenter. The energy of the electrons, however, decreases.

prompt: Instead of elongating, an octahedral complex shortens its two axial (z-axis) bonds. How does this change the d orbital energies compared with an elongation?

choices.text: The pattern reverses: dz2, dxz and dyz are raised
The pattern is the same: dz2, dxz and dyz are still lowered
choices.why: Bringing the axial ligands closer strengthens interactions along z, so the orbitals with z character rise rather than fall.

choices.text: Only dxy changes energy
choices.why: dxy lies in the xy plane; the orbitals that respond to the z-axis ligands are dz2, dxz and dyz.

choices.text: No orbital changes energy, because compression doesn't lower the symmetry
choices.why: Compressing two bonds relative to the others lowers the symmetry just as elongation does, splitting the degenerate sets.

explanation: Elongation lowers the orbitals that interact with ligands along z. Shortening the axial bonds does the opposite: dz2, dxz and dyz are elevated, and the in-plane orbitals drop to keep the barycenter.

prompt: EXAFS data for [Cu(OH2)6](BrO3)2 show two different Cu–O distances, 1.96 Å and 2.32 Å. By what percentage is the longer distance greater than the shorter one?
explanation: (2.32 Å − 1.96 Å)/1.96 Å × 100% = 0.36/1.96 × 100% = 18.4%, roughly the 20% difference the section notes between bonds that would all be the same length in a regular octahedron.

prompt: Besides changes in bond length, what other consequences of the Jahn–Teller effect does the section describe?

choices.text: Two distinct d–d absorption bands instead of one, and greater lability of octahedral Cu(II) complexes
A single, sharper d–d band and slower ligand exchange
choices.why: The extra orbital levels give two bands rather than one, and weakened axial bonds make Cu(II) complexes more labile.

choices.text: Loss of all paramagnetism in the distorted complex
choices.why: The section doesn't link the distortion to magnetism; it describes split absorption bands and increased lability.

choices.text: Two d–d bands, but only if the ground state distorts
choices.why: Two bands also appear if the excited state, rather than the ground state, undergoes a Jahn–Teller distortion.

explanation: Distortion creates additional orbital levels, so some octahedral complexes show two distinct d–d bands rather than the single band expected for pure octahedral symmetry; this also happens when only the excited state distorts. The effect is also thought to promote the lability of octahedral Cu(II) complexes by weakening the axial bonds.
